one_liner: Java GOV minimal perfect hash (F3 linear systems, ~2.2 bits/key) with C lookup; about 2x faster lookups than CMPH's CHD.
what_it_does: GOVMinimalPerfectHashFunction maps a static set of n distinct keys (strings, byte arrays or longs, via a TransformationStrategy) one-to-one onto 0..n-1 in about 2.2 bits/key, without storing the keys. It is a Java Object2LongFunction: you build it with a Builder (keys, transform, optional signature width, temp dir), serialize it, and query it with getLong(key). It does not replace CMPH directly. Construction runs only in Java, and to get native lookups you call dump() and load the file with the bare-bones C code in c/mph.c (mph_get_uint64_t, mph_get_byte_array, mph_get_uint128_t).
how_it_is_fast: Each key is hashed once with SpookyHash into a 128-bit signature and assigned to a bucket of about 1,500 keys. Each bucket is a random 3-regular linear system over F3 (Genuzio-Ottaviano-Vigna, SEA 2016), with about 10% more variables than equations, solved by hypergraph peeling plus lazy Gaussian elimination. A lookup reads the bucket's offset, then three 2-bit values whose sum mod 3 picks the key's vertex, then ranks that vertex with a broadword popcount of nonzero 2-bit pairs. After the offset read, all memory access stays inside one bucket's ~1,650 cells (~52 words), and construction scales because signatures are bucket-sorted on disk and buckets are solved in parallel.
when_to_use: JVM services that need a static map from keys to dense IDs (0..n-1) for 10^7 to 10^9+ strings, byte arrays or longs at about 2.2 bits/key, e.g. to index a term dictionary or an ID column into flat arrays.

Key sets larger than RAM. BucketedHashStore bucket-sorts 128-bit signatures into disk segments and needs under 0.75 bits/key of main memory while sorting. Each ~1,500-key bucket is then solved on its own.
Building offline in Java and querying from C/C++: dump() the function, then call mph_get_uint64_t, mph_get_byte_array or mph_get_uint128_t from c/mph.c.
Replacing CMPH's CHD when 0.06-0.22 extra bits/key is acceptable. In return you get about 2x faster lookups and 2.3-27x faster single-core construction (875 s vs 1,972-23,746 s at 10^9 keys).
Cases that also need a membership test: signed(w) stores a w-bit signature per key, so a non-member returns -1 except with probability 2^-w.
when_not_to_use: Lookup speed is the priority in native code. In the same Table 5 (10^9 keys), PTHash answers in 37-64 ns/key and BBHash gamma=2 in 143 ns/key, vs 175 ns/key for GOV.
Space is the priority. CHD lambda=6 (2.01 bits/key) and RecSplit l=8, b=100 (1.80 bits/key at 204 ns/key, 936 s to build) are both smaller than GOV's 2.23 bits/key.
Pure C/C++ or Rust projects that must build the function at runtime. Construction exists only in Java, so you need a JVM plus a dump/load step.
Dynamic sets. The structure is static, so any insert or delete means a full rebuild.
Small, cache-resident sets. At 10^6 keys (RecSplit paper Table 1), GOV's 58 ns/key trails BBHash gamma=1 (33 ns) and RecSplit l=5, b=5 (47 ns), and its lead over CHD (91-92 ns) shrinks to about 1.6x.

integration.form: module: Maven Central jar it.unimi.dsi:sux4j, latest release 5.4.1 (March 2023). The optional C lookup is a source-drop: c/mph.c, mph.h, spooky.c, spooky.h.
integration.dependencies: Java: fastutil, dsiutils, slf4j-api (logback at runtime), JSAP, commons-math3, commons-collections4, commons-lang3. C lookup: only libc/libm.
integration.min_toolchain: Java 9+ (CHANGES 5.2.3; the POM targets 1.9), built with Ant + Ivy. The C lookup needs GCC/Clang extensions (__uint128_t, __builtin_popcountll, __builtin_clzll); comp.sh uses gcc -O3 -march=native.
integration.platforms: Any JVM. The C lookup needs a 64-bit GCC/Clang target with __uint128_t. dump() writes native byte order, so load the file on a machine with the same endianness. The optional USE_MMAP path uses Linux MAP_HUGETLB.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for lookups. getLong() allocates its own scratch arrays and only reads fields set at construction, and the reporter of issue #2 shares one instance across threads. Construction is internally multithreaded: min(4, cores) threads by default, overridable with the system property it.unimi.dsi.sux4j.mph.threads.

gotchas: A key outside the build set gets an arbitrary index in [0, n), not an error, unless you build with signed(w). containsKey() always returns true.

You cannot choose the indices. Values stored in a BucketedHashStore passed to the builder are ignored (issue #3). For key-to-value static functions use GOV3Function or GOV4Function, which are not MPHFs.

The C lookup code does no validation. Nothing checks that the dump matches the key type or transformation strategy: the uint64_t tests expect RAW_LONG, the byte_array tests RAW_BYTE_ARRAY. Also, the c/ sources are LGPL-3.0-or-later, not the Java code's LGPL-2.1+/Apache-2.0.

Java getLong() still allocates a long[2] and an int[3] per call; a user flagged the GC pressure in issue #2. Construction logs heavily unless you configure the SLF4J backend (issue #11). It needs a temp directory for disk segments and throws IllegalArgumentException if duplicates persist after several rebuilds.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick GOV when you are on the JVM and want a Maven-packaged MPHF that scales past RAM, with optional signatures. minperf, the other Java sibling, claims 'very similar' performance but calls itself work in progress and was last pushed in 2021. In native C/C++, Table 5 shows PTHash at 37-64 ns/key, and RecSplit (Sux) at 1.80 bits/key with similar lookup (204 ns) and build time (936 s), so GOV mainly makes sense there if Sux4J already builds your functions.
verified_claims_summary: PTHash paper Table 5 (SIGIR'21, mirrored in mphf_benchmark): 10^9 uniformly random 64-bit keys on one core of an i9-9900K (gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native). GOV averaged 175 ns/key over every input key at 2.23 bits/key, vs 416-419 ns/key for CMPH's CHD (lambda=4-6, 2.01-2.17 bits/key), about 2.4x; at 10^8 keys it was 110 vs 197-204 ns/key, about 1.8x. GOV was built in Java and neither paper names its lookup harness (presumably Sux4J's C code). The RecSplit paper (i7-7770, gcc 8.1.1, Java 12, 128-bit random keys) independently measured 210 vs 444-447 ns/key at 10^9 keys.
status_note: Still receiving commits (C benchmark harnesses in May 2026), but the last Maven Central release is 5.4.1 from March 2023. The jar is the practical way in, and the C lookup files are small enough to vendor.
